questions.question: Write a short note on chromatography in forensic toxicology.
questions.solution_html:
• Write a short note on chromatography in forensic toxicology.
  • Chromatography is a separation technique used to separate components of a mixture based on their different interactions with
  • stationary and mobile phases. It helps detect and identify drugs, poisons, and their metabolites in biological samples such as
  • blood and urine. Common techniques include thin-layer chromatography (TLC), gas chromatography (GC), and high-
  • performance liquid chromatography (HPLC).

questions.question: Write a short account of cocaine and amphetamine type stimulants.
questions.solution_html:
• Write a short account of cocaine and amphetamine type stimulants.
  • Cocaine is a naturally occurring stimulant obtained from the leaves of the coca plant. It stimulates the central nervous system
  • by increasing the availability of neurotransmitters, particularly dopamine. Effects include euphoria, increased alertness, raised
  • heart rate, and increased blood pressure. Toxic effects include seizures, cardiac arrhythmias, and heart attack.
  • Amphetamine-type stimulants are synthetic or semi -synthetic central nervous system stimulants. Examples include
  • amphetamine, methamphetamine, and MDMA (ec stasy). They increase the activity of neurotransmitters such as dopamine
  • and noradrenaline; MDMA also strongly affects serotonin. Adverse effects include insomnia, agitation, hyperthermia,
  • hypertension, and dependence.

questions.final_answer: hypertension, and dependence.

questions.question: Describe the emergency care measures provided to patients with acute poisoning.
questions.solution_html:
• Describe the emergency care measures provided to patients with acute poisoning.
  • Ensure safety - Protect the patient and medical personnel from further exposure. Identify the suspected poison, route of
  • exposure, and time of exposure, if possible.
  • Assess and stabilise vital functions - Follow the ABC approach: airway, breathing, and circulation. Provide oxygen, assisted
  • ventilation, or CPR when clinically indicated.
  • Prevent further absorption - Remove contaminated clothing and wash exposed skin or eyes with appropriate amounts of
  • water. Do not induce vomiting routinely. Gastrointestinal decontamination, such as activated charcoal, should be considered
  • only when clinically appropriate and under medical guidance.
  • Administer specific treatment - Give an appropriate antidote when indicated, such as naloxone for suspected opioid-induced
  • respiratory depression. Treat seizures, shock, abnormal temperature, and other complications.
  • Monitor and investigate - Monitor vital signs, consciousness, ECG, and relevant laboratory paramet ers. Contact a poison
  • information centre or clinical toxicologist and arrange hospital observation or admission as needed.
questions.source_exam: V Semester MGU UGP (Honours) - 2024 Admission regular Examination October 2026
questions.final_answer: information centre or clinical toxicologist and arrange hospital observation or admission as needed.

questions.question: Explain addition and condensation polymerisation with mechanism and forensic examples.
questions.solution_html:
• Explain addition and condensation polymerisation with mechanism and forensic examples.
  • Addition polymerization - A process in which unsaturated monomers combine to form a polymer without eliminating small
  • molecules. Mechanism: Commonly proceeds through initiation, propagation, and termination in chain -growth
  • polymerisation. Example: Ethylene forms polyethylene. n CH2=CH2→ [−CH2−CH2−]n
  • Forensic examples: Polyethylene packaging, polypropylene fibres, and acrylic plastic fragments recovered from crime scenes.
  • Condensation polymerization - A process in which monomers containing suitable functional groups combine, commonly
  • with the el imination of small molecules such as water or methanol. Mechanism: Functional groups react stepwise to form
  • new covalent bonds and progressively longer polymer chains.
  • Example: Formation of a polyester from a diol and a dicarboxylic acid, with elimination of water.
  • Diol+Dicarboxylic acid→Polyester+Water
  • Forensic examples: Polyester textile fibres and nylon fibres recovered from clothing, questioned fabrics, or crime scenes.
questions.source_exam: V Semester MGU UGP (Honours) - 2024 Admission regular Examination October 2026
questions.final_answer: Forensic examples: Polyester textile fibres and nylon fibres recovered from clothing, questioned fabrics, or crime scenes.

questions.question: Explain the collection, preservation, and packing of fire debris.
questions.solution_html:
• Explain the collection, preservation, and packing of fire debris.
  • Collection - Document the fire scene with photographs, notes, and a sketch before collecting samples. Collect representative
  • debris from suspected points of origin, including materials that may contain ignitable-liquid residues. Collect a control sample
  • from an unaffected area for comparison.
  • Preservation - Minimise handling and exposure to air to reduce the loss of volatile compounds. Use clean tools and avoid
  • cross-contamination between samples. Collect samples promptly and follow laboratory protocols for volatile -residue
  • evidence.
  • Packing - Place debris in clean, airtight, vapour-resistant containers, such as approved metal cans or suitable glass containers
  • with tight closures. Avoid ordinary plastic bags because volatile residues may escape or interact with the packaging. Seal
  • each container securely and label it with the case number, sample description, location, date, time, and collector's details.
  • Documentation and transport - Maintain a complete chain-of-custody record. Store and transport samples under appropriate
  • conditions, away from heat and ignition sources. Submit samples to the forensic laboratory for examination, commonly by
  • headspace analysis and GC-MS.
  • Forensic significance - Fire debris analysis can help detect and identify ignitable-liquid residues and assist in evaluating the
  • possible origin and cause of a fire.
questions.source_exam: V Semester MGU UGP (Honours) - 2024 Admission regular Examination October 2026
questions.final_answer: possible origin and cause of a fire.

questions.question: Explain sensitivity and stability of explosives. Part D Essay Questions
questions.solution_html:
• Explain sensitivity and stability of explosives.
  • Sensitivity of explosives - Sensitivity is the degree to which an explosive responds to an external stimulus and initiates a
  • reaction or detonation. Impact sensitivity: Response to mechanical impact. Friction sensitivity: Response to frictional force.
  • Thermal sensitivity: Response to heat or elevated temperature.
  • Importance: Sensitivity influences the hazards associated with handling, transport, storage, and accidental initiation.
  • Stability of explosives - Stability is the ability of an explosive to retain its chemical and physical properties during storage
  • and handling.
  • Chemical stability: Resistance to decomposition over time. Thermal stability: Ability to resist heat-induced decomposition.
  • Environmental stability: Resistance to deterioration due to moisture, light, and other environmental conditions.
  • Importance: Stable explosives are generally safer to store under approved conditions, while deterioration may increase
  • hazards or reduce performance.
  • Relationship between sensitivity and stability - Sensitivity describes how readily an explosive initiates in response to a
  • stimulus. Stability describes how we ll it resists unwanted change or decomposition over time. They are distinct properties:
  • an explosive may be relatively stable during proper storage yet sensitive to a particular initiating stimulus.
  • Forensic importance: These properties help forensic experts assess explosive hazards, examine damaged or recovered
  • materials, and interpret evidence from explosion scenes.
  • Part D
  • Essay Questions

questions.question: Describe the general management of poisoning. Explain the emergency care of poisoned patients, including stabilization, decontamination, supportive care, and enhanced elimination of poisons.
questions.solution_html:
• Describe the general management of poisoning. Explain the emergency care of poisoned patients, including
  • stabilization, decontamination, supportive care, and enhanced elimination of poisons.
  • Initial assessment: Identify the suspected poison, route of exposure, and time of poisoning. Stabilization: Maintain airway,
  • breathing, and circulation using the ABCDE approach. Decontamination: Remove contaminated clothing, wash exposed skin,
  • irrigate eyes, and use activated charcoal when appropriate. Do not induce vomiting. Supportive care: Monitor vital signs and
  • treat seizures, shock, respiratory failure, and metabolic disturbances. Antidotes: Administer specific antidotes when indicated,
  • such as naloxone for opioid poisoning and N-acetylcysteine for paracetamol poisoning. Enhanced elimination: Use selected
  • methods such as urinary alkalinisation, multiple-dose activated charcoal, or haemodialysis when appropriate.
  • Early stabilization, appropriate treatment, and continuous monitoring are essential for successful management.
questions.source_exam: V Semester MGU UGP (Honours) - 2024 Admission regular Examination October 2026
questions.final_answer: Early stabilization, appropriate treatment, and continuous monitoring are essential for successful management.

questions.question: Compare composition based dating information with aging based measurements. Explain what each can contribute and why neither always provides a precise writing date.
questions.solution_html:
• Compare composition based dating information with aging based measurements. Explain what each can
  • contribute and why neither always provides a precise writing date.
  • Composition-based dating: Examines ink ingredients, such as dyes, pigments, solvents, and resins, to identify the formulation
  • and establish possible chronological limits. Aging-based measurements: Examine changes in ink over time, such as solvent
  • evaporation, oxidation, and chemical degradation. Methods used: Chemical analysis, including GC–MS, may help examine
  • ink composition or selected aging -related changes. Comparison: Composition-based analysis studies what the ink contains,
  • whereas aging-based analysis studies how the ink changes over time. Limitations: Ink formulations may be used for years,
  • while environmental conditions such as heat, humid ity, and light affect aging. Neither method always establishes the exact
  • writing date. Results must be interpreted with other forensic evidence and the limitations of the analytical method.
questions.source_exam: V Semester MGU UGP (Honours) - 2024 Admission regular Examination October 2026
questions.final_answer: writing date. Results must be interpreted with other forensic evidence and the limitations of the analytical method.
